a5749.en:
Children have their own special language for expressing their love for the people around them, though it is rare for people to understand that language. Our children love us sincerely, even if they cannot always say so in words, or show it through actions.

Understanding their love language can help strengthen our relationship with them and make them feel safe and valued.

The concept of the American author Dr Gary Chapman regarding the five love languages - which are physical touch, words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, and acts of service - can be applied to children too. Understanding their love language helps us connect with them in a way that is more comprehensible to them.

As is the case with us adults, children also show their love in various ways, even if not in direct words. They may seek physical closeness through hugging, or holding hands, smiling and laughing when we are present, or even imitating our behaviour as a sign of their love.

Also, when they look at us in the eyes with joy, or bring us a small gift of the things they love such as a drawing or a doll, they are demonstrating their feelings of love. Sometimes, children show love by wanting more time together with us, or by seeking comfort when they are sad.

READ MORE: How Can We Talk to Our Children About the Issue of Relationships?

The five love languages

Every child has their own unique way of expressing and receiving love. Recognising this helps us develop a deep emotional relationship with our children.

Touch - Children who prefer this language receive and express love through being hugged, being cuddled, and holding hands. Gestures such as touching the back, or back pats, gently, or a goodnight kiss make them feel safe and loved.

Words of encouragement and affirmation - Praise and encouraging words such as "We love you," "I am proud to have a child like you," or "You are special," or clapping for them and cheering them joyfully when they accomplish something, increase a child's self-confidence and make them feel valued.

Quality Time - Children who value this language love to share special time with us, whether by playing, reading together, or face-to-face conversations. Our attention to them when we are together - especially caring, listening and showing cooperation - builds a good emotional relationship.

Gifts - Children who receive love through gifts value even small gestures such as a card with a loving message. What matters most is not the value of the gift, but the intention behind that gift.

READ MORE: How Can We Protect Our Children Online?

Acts of service - Children love to show love by taking part in helping with chores even if they cannot do them well, so showing them cooperation by not discouraging them, and helping a child with schoolwork, cooking them their favourite food, or fixing their broken doll are ways of showing love through actions rather than words.

Every child has one main love language, but they may also value elements of the other languages.

We can discover their love language by observing their behaviour: Do they like hugging/being hugged or holding hands? (Physical touch); Do they like to hear encouraging words? (Words of affirmation); Do they like to have special time with us or with their friends? (Quality time); Do they like to bring us small gifts or to receive gifts? (Gifts); and Do they like to help us or help their peers with small tasks? (Acts of service).

Understanding these signs helps us build a deep emotional relationship with our children. It is also important to understand that a child's love language can change as they grow. Being attentive to these changes ensures that they feel loved and valued at all times.

So let us learn to communicate in their love language, so that we build a solid foundation of a relationship built on trust, safety, compassion and love. Children who know they are loved grow up confident, compassionate, and with feelings of being valued.

These parenting articles are prepared by C-Sema, a non-governmental organisation focused on promoting and protecting children's rights in Tanzania. For comments and advice, call them on telephone number 116, which is dedicated to child services. This service is free of charge from all networks in the country. You can also reach them through their Facebook page: Sema Tanzania, X: @SemaTanzania, and through their website www.sematanzania.org.

NAIROBI, 27 March 2027 (Eye Radio) – The Kenyan government is calling on South Sudanese peace parties to prioritize peace in the country by returning to implementation of the 2018 peace agreement.
The Cabinet Secretary for Foreign and Diaspora Affairs, Dr. Musalia Mudavadi said the Kenyan government is “concerned with the developments in South Sudan following reports of the detention of FVP, Dr, Riek Machar on March 26.”
Mudavadi called on South Sudanese leaders to exercise utmost restraint, cease hostilities, and uphold the peace agreement as a way of putting the interest of millions of people above their own.
South Sudan has experienced a deteriorating security situation and a breakdown in working relationship among the 2018 peace parties following the outbreak of violence in Nasir in Upper Nile, Western Equatoria and Western Bahr el Ghazal.
On Tuesday, Kenya’s President William Ruto said he discussed the current security situation in South Sudan in a telephone conversation with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
On Wednesday, First Vice President Dr. Riek Machar was put under “house arrest” in Juba, according to his party, as UN warns that the country stands on the brink of return to civil war.
The U.S. Department of State’s Bureau of Africa Affairs expressed concern on Thursday over the detention of Machar and called on President Salva Kiir to reverse the decision to prevent further escalation.

Improved climate conditions, government policy and strategic interventions as well as strong drought-mitigating strategies played a crucial role in Namibia’s reclassification as a hunger hotspot.
Namibia has since been removed from the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) of the United Nations and the World Food Programme (WFP) 2025 lists of the World Hunger Hotspots.
The identification of hunger hotspots is based on a forward-looking analysis that highlights where acute food insecurity is most likely to significantly worsen. This process is grounded in consensus among food security experts, conflict analysts and specialists in economics and natural hazards from both FAO and WFP at headquarters and in the field.
FAO and WFP, which are both UN agencies, release annual lists of the world’s most severe hunger hotspots.
These include countries and territories where acute food insecurity is likely to worsen during a specific outlook period.
In its latest report, the two agencies reclassified Namibia as a more stable and food-secure country, which saw it being removed from the 2025 World Hunger Hotspots list along with Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
“Although these countries are no longer considered hotspots for the outlook period, future climatic shifts could lead to their reclassification,” the report states.
In Southern Africa, although climatic conditions have improved compared to 2024, when the region experienced widespread and intense drought, a combination of flooding, cyclones and dry spells in some areas is likely to continue posing a significant risk to food insecurity.
The classification process is grounded in consensus among food security experts, conflict analysts and specialists in economics as well as natural hazards from both FAO and WFP in the field.
The hotspot identification is informed by an initial prioritisation using a set of quantitative and qualitative indicators.
In other jurisdictions, the report shows that acute food insecurity is likely to worsen across 13 countries and territories identified as hotspots. As such, urgent humanitarian action is needed in these hotspots, with Sudan, Palestine, South Sudan, Haiti and Mali being the highest of concern and requiring urgent attention. Yemen, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Myanmar and Nigeria are also classified as hotspots of very high concern and require urgent attention to prevent further deterioration of livelihoods.
The other identified hotspots are Burkina Faso, Chad, Somalia and the Syrian Arab Republic.
Interventions
Last year, Namibia faced one of its worst and most crippling droughts ever recorded, with farmers countrywide losing hundreds of livestock and crop fields.
As part of its strategic intervention, the government provided a budget of N$1.6 billion through its drought relief programme, which helped shield 1.2 million drought-stricken citizens from a looming hunger crisis.
Through the allocation, the government was able to reach an estimated 373 276 households nationwide, which translated into 41% of the country’s population.
The budget was rolled out in multiple phases of drought aid, which included food assistance to vulnerable households, cash incentives for livestock farmers and water provision for drought-hit communities.
The protracted drought also saw the country’s aggregated cereal production of white maize, sorghum, pearl millet and wheat decrease by 53%, while dam levels countrywide dropped to an alarming 69.7%.
As a result of the diminishing crop output and declining dam levels, there was a significant deterioration in household food security in various regions of the country for most of last year.
Additional government interventions to turn around the situation included providing drought-resistant seeds and modern agricultural training to communal farmers, increasing capacity-building initiatives for agricultural extension officers and expanding hydroponic fodder production across all regions.
The State also continued with monitoring key factors such as staple commodity prices, inflation impacts, seasonal rainfall patterns and the potential effects of La Niña to mitigate future crises as well as ensure timely and effective humanitarian assistance.
Statistics
In its July/September 2024 report, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) stated that about 1.2 million people, which is about 38% of Namibia’s population, were classified in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis) or above.
This necessitated urgent humanitarian assistance to mitigate food consumption gaps and protect livelihoods.
The analysis was conducted in three phases.
The first phase was in October 2023, the second between April and June 2024 and the last phase from July to September 2024.
Despite slight improvements, the food security situation in the country was expected to deteriorate during the lean season of October 2024 to March 2025.
It was anticipated to affect an estimated 1.2 million people.
The IPC report attributed the ongoing crisis to several key factors, including climate shocks, particularly the impact of El Niño, which led to erratic rainfall and prolonged drought, severely affecting crop and livestock production across all 14 regions of Namibia.
The report highlighted deteriorating livestock conditions, with some regions such as Kunene suffering significant livestock deaths due to disease outbreaks and poor condition of pastures.
It warned that national food levels are critically low, with silos holding just 15% of their total capacity as of June 2024, further underscoring the severity of the crisis.

a6133.t:
It's Monday morning 08:00 Dr Thembisile Xulu, just off the red-eye from Durban, is about to hit the road to Limpopo in preparation for World Aids Day. A year had passed since Spotlightinterviewed her shortly after her appointment as CEO of the South African National AIDS Council (SANAC) in October last year.
During last year's interview, Xulu described herself saying, "When I sit in a room, I don't necessarily regard myself as the smartest. In fact, mostly I'm not. I thrive when I manage people who are smarter than me. My job is to inspire and to drive the bus. But I need team members holding the GPS to say ‘driver, this thing is not going the right way, we need to go there or there'."
Having now been in the driver's seat at SANAC for a year, Xulu stresses that an integrated approach is key to fighting the "colliding epidemics" of our time. She was speaking from her Johannesburg home, with a SANAC poster behind her.
"Our theme for World Aids Day this year is working together to end inequalities in Aids, TB, and Covid-19," she says. "Our tagline is - Get tested. Get vaccinated. Adhere to treatment. Essentially, it is meant to bring together all these colliding epidemics we have - HIV, TB, and Covid-19.
"So if you get tested; you not only know your HIV status or your TB status; you know your hypertension, your blood pressure, your cholesterol, your Covid status, and you also get vaccinated."
Tapping into traditional leadership
At SANAC's World Aids Day gathering in Xukundu Village in Limpopo, Deputy President David Mabuza as SANAC chairperson will give the keynote address. Xulu says that to really successfully convey their message at grassroots level - in order to really shift perceptions - collaborating with traditional leaders is key.
"We need to tap into the power and the strength that traditional leaders have," she says. "Our traditional leaders are holding indabas and they're holding meetings with their communities. And if they are the ones that are constantly speaking about HIV and TB and Covid-19, people will listen."
Xulu grew up in the Durban township of Inanda and can relate.
"I come from that life and I know how well respected the King or the chief is. In Zulu, there's a saying that if something comes from the mouth of the chief, it's golden, it's taken as the truth. So we are tapping into that," she says.
Coordinating donors
Amongst other things, SANAC hosts South Africa's Global Fund Country Coordinating Mechanism (CCM). This means the council is responsible for interfacing with international donors on South Africa's behalf; then allocating and tracking funding running into billions of rands.
Asked about the scope of international funding, Xulu points out that The Global Fund [The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria] will allocate $536 million to South Africa over a three-year period, starting April 2022. PEPFAR [the United States President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief] will allocate over $435 million this year alone.
Pushed on the specifics of this function, she says: "SANAC's role is to make sure that the council galvanises all the stakeholders towards the implementation of the NSP [National Strategic Plan]. We are not the ones who directly get the money. But we ensure optimal allocation, non-duplication and we measure outcomes and performance. The ‘principal recipients' of The Global Fund answer to us on a monthly basis."
SANAC is also the forum through which South Africa's National Strategic Plan (NSP) for HIV, TB, and STIs is developed. Currently, the 2017-2022 plan is in effect - mapping the measurable goals set for the country's fight against HIV, TB, and STIs.
Due to backlogs created by Covid-19, Xulu says the current NSP will be extended to 2023 with "catch-up plans" across sectors.
In recent years it has at times appeared that key HIV policies are determined inside the Department of Health or by guideline committees without SANAC necessarily playing a meaningful role. Asked whether SANAC actually has an impact on HIV policy in South Africa, Xulu responds that SANAC brings together various stakeholders in formulating HIV policy.
"SANAC is a body established by cabinet to ensure that there is a multi-sectorial response to HIV and it is located in the highest office in the country - the Presidency," she says. "The goal is [getting] everyone to realise that HIV is not just a health problem.
"HIV requires all sectors of society. That's why the plenary of SANAC is composed of government, of civil society, of the private sector, of development partners, of labour, etcetera. For example, the mining sector is rife with TB. So the Department of Minerals and Energy sits on SANAC."
Better coordination around health needed
She illustrates the interrelatedness of cultural norms and transmission, citing findings from a recent TB prevalence survey. "We found that men have a higher incidence of TB than women," she says. "So, men's health-seeking behaviour is very low. I probably don't have the right words for men. Men don't want to test, you know.
"Men still use their wives as proxies to test for HIV. They say my wife is negative, which means I'm negative. Men don't want to be on treatment. Men just don't want anything to do with health facilities. As a result, for instance, let's just say he's got Covid. It means he's coming home to his family, every day and spreading it. Maybe he's got HIV and he refuses to test. It means if he's in a rural area where polygamy is a thing, he's still spreading HIV to all his wives."
As a further illustration, she points out the StatsSA findings published last month showing that 688 girls aged nine to ten years old gave birth in South Africa in 2020.
"It is unacceptable, completely unacceptable," says Xulu. "So yes, at this weekend's plenary, the Department of Basic Education presented a learner pregnancy management strategy that has been adopted by cabinet. They essentially got a whole package of services aligned to make sure that girls are strengthened in and out of schools.
"But the key thing is that there's no nine or ten-year-old that falls pregnant in the classroom. Research shows that our young girls are impregnated by older men. And these older men need to be held accountable by the law, which means there needs to be better collaboration.
"And I speak really as a SANAC multi-sectoral administrator. There needs to be better collaboration around health, starting at the school. When the school is aware that there's a pregnant girl and she is underage, you know, by the time she gets to deliver, health needs to report that to the department of social development - the custodian of children - and then involve the police services, too."
South Africa's influence
Xulu says that South Africa and our NSP are significant in a regional context.
"In June, we went to the United Nations high-level meeting on HIV and AIDS for Africa where each member state actually put forward their declaration towards ending HIV. And you find that there are countries that actually really rely on the voice of South Africa when it comes to issues of human rights, LGBTQ issues, or issues relating to other key populations that still find themselves being persecuted because of the laws that these countries follow," she says.
"So people rely on South Africa because we've got such a strong Constitution. And our NSP is very clear in terms of key populations that nobody should be left behind. For example, you'll find that men who have sex with men are not legally acceptable in many countries in Africa."
A push in South Africa to have sex work decriminalised is pioneering within a broader regional context, too. "You know, on 28 October 2021, we launched a sex worker plan, which speaks to the needs of sex workers," says Xulu. "The fact that they need to be able to access condoms. They need to be able to test, they need to be able to get treatment, and they need to be recognised as a trade, in essence."
"The sex worker sector actually warned SANAC that this was the last plan that was being signed without decriminalising sex work," she adds. "The sex worker plan is a complementary document to the NSP for TB/HIV, and STI's, similar to the LGBTQI plan…"
Before taking over the reins at SANAC a year ago, Xulu worked for 16 years at HIV treatment non-profit organisation, Right to Care. Before that, she did perinatal HIV research at the Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital in Johannesburg.
*This article was produced by Spotlight - health journalism in the public interest.

a6263.t:
Minister of Finance, Simplex Chithyola Banda, has strongly dismissed as false and malicious the claims circulating on social media suggesting that government plans to devalue the Malawi kwacha by 150% after the elections.
“These are fabrications by disgruntled individuals bent on tarnishing government’s image,” Chithyola Banda said. “The so-called cabinet paper making rounds is not signed, lacks context, and is clearly a desperate attempt to mislead the public.”
The Minister’s remarks follow a similar statement from the Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM), which recently denied any plans for devaluation. RBM Governor, Dr. Mafuta Mwale, stressed that the central bank’s focus is not on currency devaluation but on stabilising the economy through inflation control and improved foreign exchange supply.
Dr. Mwale noted that inflation has been falling for four consecutive months and highlighted government’s interventions such as maize imports to cushion food prices. He described the rumours as “fake news designed to sow panic” and urged Malawians to pay attention to tangible economic progress rather than fear-mongering.
The document in circulation — falsely presented as a cabinet paper dated August 2025 — claims that President Lazarus Chakwera intends to devalue the kwacha, increase fuel prices by 100%, retrench public service workers, and raise PAYE. Government has dismissed all these allegations as outright lies.
As Malawians prepare to cast their votes on September 16 for President, Members of Parliament, and councillors, analysts warn that such fake news is a deliberate ploy by opposition elements to manipulate public opinion and erode trust in government.
Officials maintain that Malawi’s economic recovery efforts remain on track, and that spreading baseless rumours of massive devaluation is not only irresponsible but also a direct attack on the stability of the nation’s financial system.

a6273.t:
President John Dramani Mahama has urged African leaders to back the full rollout of the proposed African Monetary Fund and other regional financial institutions to help reduce the continent’s reliance on foreign borrowing and ease pressure on foreign exchange reserves.
Addressing the First African Union Debt Conference in Lomé, Togo, on Monday, May 12, 2025, President Mahama said African countries like Ghana need stronger regional alternatives to the current global financial system, which he described as structurally tilted against the continent.
“Our countries need access to long-term, affordable finance, but the global financial system remains structurally unfair to Africa,” Mr Mahama said. “We must strengthen African financial institutions like the AfriExim Bank, the African Development Bank, and the proposed African Monetary Fund to offer concessional financing that reflects Africa’s realities.”
The conference, which brought together heads of state, finance ministers, AU commissioners and development partners, was convened to discuss how African nations can manage rising debt while protecting development goals.
Mr Mahama described the current debt conditions facing many African countries as unsustainable, pointing to Ghana’s own experience in recent years. He said poor decisions, especially between 2017 and 2022, had driven Ghana into a difficult debt crisis.
“Ghana, like many of our peers, is still recovering from a painful debt restructuring process,” he noted. “We saw our debt-to-GDP ratio rise sharply due to a combination of excessive borrowing and weak governance.”
According to him, African countries spent over US$90 billion servicing debt in 2024 alone, nearly twice what the continent receives annually in foreign aid, and more than many governments spend on health and education combined.
Mr Mahama said Africa must stop borrowing simply to fill budget gaps and instead direct loans toward productive investments that create jobs, expand exports and strengthen public services.
“Debt must serve the people,” he stated. “That means stronger parliamentary oversight, regular public audits, and greater transparency in how loans are used. Less than 40 per cent of African countries currently publish detailed debt reports. That must change.”
Mr Mahama outlined three main principles for a new approach to public debt management: transparency and accountability, responsible borrowing tied to specific investments, and regional cooperation to secure better financial terms.
He announced that Ghana is moving to establish an independent fiscal council to provide real-time oversight of borrowing decisions and public spending.
He also said the government intends to expand the mandate of the Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund (GIIF) to help attract private capital into strategic sectors, reducing the need for risky loans.
Mr Mahama urged African countries to adopt a single negotiating position ahead of the 2025 G20 Summit, where debt restructuring for low- and middle-income countries is expected to feature prominently.
“The debt trap is not just an African problem; it reflects deeper issues in how the global financial system works,” he said.
“But we must also take responsibility for the way we borrow and spend. Debt must not be a sentence. It must be a tool for building better lives.”
The African Union Debt Conference was held under the theme “Africa’s Public Debt Management: Agenda in Restoring and Safeguarding Debt Sustainability.”
Participants discussed the state of public finances across the continent and explored ways to reduce debt burdens without halting progress in key sectors.

a6310.t:
Au mois de mars 2025, le gouvernement chinois a présenté le rapport d’activités de l’année 2024. Ce rapport met en lumière l’engagement de la Chine à élargir la politique d’ouverture parmi les activités inscrites sur le programme d’activités de l’année 2025. L’approfondissement de la coopération économique bilatérale, multilatérale et régionale ainsi que l’encouragement des investissements étrangers sont au cœur du gouvernement chinois.
« Elargir l’ouverture sur l’extérieur de haut niveau, stabiliser le commerce extérieur et les investissements étrangers sont parmi les priorités de la Chine. Quels que soient les changements extérieurs, nous persisterons dans la pratique de l’ouverture », lit-on sur le rapport d’activités du gouvernement chinois approuvé le 11 mars 2025 lors de la troisième session de la 14e Assemblée populaire nationale.
Concernant la stabilisation du développement du commerce extérieur, la Chine s’est engagée à intensifier ses politiques dans ce domaine, à améliorer les services financiers en aidant aussi les entreprises chinoises qui participent à des expositions ou organisent des expositions à l’étranger.
« Nous promouvrons le développement du cybercommerce transfrontalier, améliorerons le système d’expédition rapide transfrontalière et renforcerons la construction de nos entrepôts à l’étranger», poursuit ce rapport d’activités. Pour arriver à ce niveau, on prévoit la multiplication des fonctions des zones de coopération économique et commerciale à l’étranger, le développement du commerce des biens intermédiaires et la recherche à diversifier le marché. La promotion du développement innovant du commerce des services est également au cœur du gouvernement chinois. « Nous créerons de nouveaux pôles de croissance tels que le commerce vert et le commerce numérique, soutiendrons les régions réunissant les conditions requises dans leur développement du commerce offshore de type nouveau, et développerons activement le commerce frontalier », précise le rapport.
Développement du concept « Investir en Chine »
Dans cette logique de promouvoir la politique d’ouverture, la Chine mettra beaucoup d’efforts dans l’organisation des foires importantes, entre autres l’exposition internationale d’importation de la Chine, la foire chinoise de l’importation et de l’exportation (Foire de Canton), la foire internationale du commerce des services de Chine, l’exposition mondiale du commerce numérique. A cela s’ajoute la construction de douanes intelligentes et le renforcement de la coopération internationale dans ce domaine pour faciliter le dédouanement.
Bien que la Chine soit une grande économie mondiale, elle laisse les portes ouvertes aux investisseurs étrangers. « Des expériences pilotes seront menées à bien pour élargir l’ouverture du secteur des services. Nous encouragerons les investisseurs étrangers à augmenter leurs réinvestissements en Chine et à participer à la coopération en amont et en aval des chaînes industrielles. Nous garantirons effectivement aux entreprises à capitaux étrangers le traitement national en ce qui concerne l’acquisition de facteurs de production, l’obtention des qualifications, l’établissement des normes et les achats publics. Nous assurerons les services aux entreprises à capitaux étrangers, accélérerons la mise en chantier de projets emblématiques et continuerons à développer le concept « Investir en Chine », a souligné ce rapport d’activités.
Parmi d’autres activités envisagées figurent la promotion de la mise à niveau des zones pilotes de libre-échange, l’optimisation des politiques en faveur de l’ouverture des zones de développement économique et technique ainsi que la création d’un environnement des affaires de premier ordre conforme à la loi chinoise, aux règles du marché et aux normes internationales. Selon ce rapport publié, tout cela permettra aux entreprises à capitaux étrangers de mieux se développer. L’approfondissement de la coopération économique bilatérale, multilatérale et régionale est également privilégié.
Source:Xinhua
Claude Hakizimana
a6310.en:
In March 2025, the Chinese government presented its work report for 2024. The report highlights China's commitment to broadening its opening-up policy among the activities included in the 2025 programme of work. Deepening bilateral, multilateral and regional economic cooperation, as well as encouraging foreign investment, are at the heart of the Chinese government's agenda.

"Expanding high-level opening up to the outside world and stabilising foreign trade and foreign investment are among China's priorities. Whatever the external changes, we will persist in the practice of opening up," reads the Chinese government's work report, approved on 11 March 2025 at the third session of the 14th National People's Congress.

As regards stabilising the development of foreign trade, China has undertaken to step up its policies in this area and to improve financial services, including by helping Chinese companies that take part in exhibitions or organise exhibitions abroad.

"We will promote the development of cross-border e-commerce, improve the cross-border express delivery system and strengthen the construction of our overseas warehouses," the work report continues. To reach this level, the plans include multiplying the functions of overseas economic and trade cooperation zones, developing trade in intermediate goods and seeking to diversify markets. Promoting the innovative development of trade in services is also central to the Chinese government's agenda. "We will create new growth poles such as green trade and digital trade, support regions that meet the requisite conditions in their development of new types of offshore trade, and actively develop border trade," the report specifies.

Development of the "Invest in China" concept

In keeping with this drive to promote the opening-up policy, China will put considerable effort into organising major fairs, among them the China International Import Expo, the China Import and Export Fair (Canton Fair), the China International Fair for Trade in Services and the Global Digital Trade Expo. Added to this is the building of smart customs facilities and the strengthening of international cooperation in this field in order to facilitate customs clearance.

Although China is a major global economy, it keeps its doors open to foreign investors. "Pilot experiments will be carried through in order to broaden the opening of the services sector. We will encourage foreign investors to increase their reinvestment in China and to take part in upstream and downstream industrial-chain cooperation. We will effectively guarantee foreign-funded enterprises national treatment with regard to the acquisition of factors of production, the obtaining of qualifications, the setting of standards and public procurement. We will provide services to foreign-funded enterprises, speed up the launch of flagship projects and continue to develop the 'Invest in China' concept," the work report stressed.

Among the other activities envisaged are promoting the upgrading of pilot free-trade zones, optimising policies in favour of opening up economic and technological development zones, and creating a first-class business environment consistent with Chinese law, market rules and international standards. According to the published report, all of this will allow foreign-funded enterprises to develop better. Deepening bilateral, multilateral and regional economic cooperation is also given priority.

Source: Xinhua
Claude Hakizimana

a6381.t:
The Trump administration’s move to gut the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) has crippled the agency’s ability to conduct any proper oversight of unspent aid worth $8.2 billion, an independent government watchdog said on Monday.
A report by the USAID Office of the Inspector-General also said that waivers issued by the State Department to make “life-saving humanitarian assistance” exempt from President Donald Trump’s freeze on U.S. foreign aid were hampered by sweeping staff cuts and uncertainty over what kind of aid is and is not permissible.
Hundreds of USAID programs covering billions of dollars of assistance across the globe came to a halt after Trump on January 20 ordered a freeze on most U.S. foreign aid, saying he wanted to ensure it was aligned with his “America First” policy.
His administration has moved to dismantle USAID, which had more than 10,000 staff at home and overseas, and possibly merge it into the State Department. The agency’s web site has been down for more than a week. But the report from the OIG, an independent oversight division of the agency, appeared on Monday on the OIG’s website, which remains online.
OIG said its report was covering the risks around the agency’s $8.2 billion of “obligated but undisbursed humanitarian assistance funds” since the administration’s halt to aid and subsequent staff cuts, both of which it said had effectively crippled USAID’s bureau of humanitarian affairs (BHA).
“Recent widespread staffing reductions across the Agency, particularly within BHA, coupled with uncertainty about the scope of foreign assistance waivers and permissible communications with implementers, has degraded USAID’s ability to distribute and safeguard taxpayer-funded humanitarian assistance,” the report said.
“Specifically, USAID’s existing oversight controls—albeit with previously identified shortcomings—are now largely
nonoperational given these recent directives and personnel actions,” it added.
USAID programs in certain countries require partner vetting and third-party monitoring to ensure that funds are delivered to those intended and do not go to “terrorists and their supporters”, but oversight mechanisms were crippled by the staff cuts, the report said.
“This gap leaves USAID susceptible to inadvertently funding entities or salaries of individuals associated with U.S.-designated terrorist organizations,” it added.
Most of USAID’s workforce was put on administrative leave last week, with the exception of around 600 people, according to a notice sent to staff last week and shared with Reuters by an administration official.
While U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued waivers for what he called “life-saving humanitarian assistance” to be exempt from the freeze, aid workers and U.N. staff said most of the programs remained shut.
The report also said “a lack of clarity about the scope of the humanitarian assistance waivers and the extent of permissible communications between BHA staff and its implementers” hampered USAID’s capacity to disburse humanitarian assistance.
The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

a6384.t:
Ethiopia's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Demeke Mekonnen, has resigned from his dual role in the government, according to state media reports.
The announcement came on Friday, January 26, 2024, without giving any reasons for his decision. Mekonnen had been serving as the Deputy Prime Minister since November 2020, when he replaced former Prime Minister Hailemariam Desalegn, who also stepped down amid political turmoil.
Mekonnen, who is from the Amhara ethnic group, was also the leader of the Amhara Democratic Party (ADP), one of the four parties that make up the ruling Prosperity Party (PP) coalition. The Amhara region has been at the center of a violent conflict between the federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), a rebel group that once dominated Ethiopian politics.
The TPLF accuses Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who is from the Oromo ethnic group, of marginalizing and persecuting the Tigrayans and other ethnic minorities. Abiy, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 for ending a long-standing border dispute with neighboring Eritrea, launched a military offensive against the TPLF in November 2020, after the group allegedly attacked a federal military base.
The war has resulted in thousands of deaths, millions of displacements, and widespread human rights violations, according to international observers. Abiy has also faced accusations of genocide and ethnic cleansing in the Amhara region, where his forces have allegedly committed atrocities against the Tigrayans and other ethnic groups.
Mekonnen's resignation comes amid growing pressure on Abiy to end the war and engage in dialogue with the TPLF and other opposition groups. The African Union, the United Nations, the European Union, and the United States have all called for a ceasefire and a peaceful resolution of the crisis.
The resignation of Mekonnen, who was seen as a moderate and a bridge-builder within the PP coalition, could signal a further deterioration of the political situation in Ethiopia and the region. It could also create a power vacuum and a leadership crisis within the ADP and the PP, which could affect the stability and legitimacy of the government.

a6510.t:
Le 25 mars, l’Union européenne marquera les 60 ans de la signature des Traités de Rome, le premier pas vers une Europe unie. Depuis la naissance des Communautés européennes en 1957, l’Europe a connu 6 décennies de paix, de prospérité et de sécurité sans précédent.
Le contraste avec la première moitié du XXème siècle ne pouvait être plus frappant. Deux guerres catastrophiques en Europe en 1914-18 et 1939-1945 ont laissé des millions de morts et un continent dévasté, divisé et prostré. Pour les pays qui étaient depuis longtemps en guerre, l’intégration européenne a été le projet de paix le plus réussi de notre histoire.
Aujourd’hui, nous vivons des temps imprévisibles. Le 60èmeanniversaire des Traités de Rome est l’occasion non seulement de réaffirmer notre attachement aux valeurs et objectifs sur lesquels le projet européen est fondé, mais aussi de prendre des mesures pragmatiques et ambitieuses.
L’Union européenne est présente au Bénin depuis son indépendance et le partenariat entre Union européenne et Bénin s’est approfondi au fil des années. Limitée à la coopération au cours des premières années voire décennies, le partenariat s’est depuis lors fortement étendu. Aujourd’hui, nous échangeons régulièrement sur des questions de politique étrangère, de sécurité, de droits de l’homme ou encore des questions d’intérêt mondial comme le changement climatique ou la mobilité.
Le monde traverse une période de grande incertitude. L’équilibre mondial se déplace et les fondements d’un ordre international basé sur des règles sont trop souvent remis en cause. Mais la position de l’UE fournit, elle, des certitudes: nous sommes défenseurs de meilleures règles mondiales, de règles qui protègent les citoyens contre les abus, de règles qui élargissent les droits et augmentent les normes. C’est grâce à notre engagement –de l’Union et de ses États Membres – que la communauté mondiale a mis en place des Accords novateurs tels que « les Objectifs de Développement Durable », « l’Accord de Paris sur le Changement Climatique » et « le Programme d’Action d’Addis-Abeba sur le Financement du Développement ». Dans un monde où la politique du pouvoir émerge, l’Union européenne aura un rôle encore plus important à jouer.
L’Union européenne est et restera un partenaire solide, coopératif et fiable. Nos partenaires connaissent nos secteurs d’activités et les valeurs que nous défendons.Nous défendons le multilatéralisme, les droits de l’homme et la coopération internationale.
L’UE est la deuxième économie mondiale. Nous sommes le plus grand marché mondial et le principal investisseur étranger dans la plupart des régions du globe. L’UE a atteint une position influente en agissant ensemble et d’une seule voix sur la scène mondiale, en jouant, en tant que membre de l’Organisation Mondiale du Commerce, un rôle clé dans l’élimination des obstacles au commerce et en concluant des accords commerciaux bilatéraux avec de nombreux partenaires importants – comme le récent accord de la CETA avec le Canada. Cela a permis aux entreprises européennes exportatrices de prospérer et de créer plus de 30 millions d’emplois.
Exemplaire original traité de Rome
Nous investissons plus dans la coopération au développement et l’aide humanitaire que le reste du monde combiné. L’UE est de plus en plus active en tant que fournisseur mondial de sécurité.Nous œuvrons pour le développement durable, des sociétés inclusives, la lutte contre toutes les inégalités – dans l’éducation, la démocratie et les droits de l’homme. L’Union européenne est le premier bailleur mondial d’aide au développement. Pour nous, ce n’est pas de la charité: c’est un investissement intelligent dans votre prospérité et stabilité et par conséquent aussi dans notre propre sécurité et prospérité.
Nous avons joué un rôle déterminant dans la planification des objectifs de développement durable de l’ONU et nous les avons déjà mis en œuvre, tout en travaillant à la mise à jour du Consensus européen sur la politique de développement. L’aide au développement de l’UE va auprès de 150 pays environ dans le monde et se concentre de plus en plus sur les régions les plus pauvres du monde. L’UE est le seul donateur à travers le monde qui apporte son soutien dans tous les pays fragiles ou en situation de conflit.
Un environnement international plus fragile appelle à un engagement accru, et non à un retranchement. C’est pourquoi l’UE continuera à soutenir et à aider les Nations Unies: notre coopération avec l’ONU porte sur les missions de paix, les efforts diplomatiques, les droits de l’homme, la lutte contre la faim et la criminalité. L’Union européenne est également un partenaire fort et actif des organisations régionales telles que l’Union Africaine, l’Association des Nations de l’Asie du Sud-Est et le Conseil de l’Arctique.
L’Union européenne est également prête à aider les personnes touchées par les catastrophes naturelles et/ou causées par l’homme. Les crises humanitaires continuent de peser lourdement sur le plan international et, en 2016, l’UE a alloué plus de 1,5 milliard d’euros à l’aide alimentaire, au logement, à la protection et aux soins de santé à 120 millions de personnes dans plus de 80 pays. Depuis le début du conflit syrien en 2011, l’UE est le plus grand bailleur de l’aide humanitaire pour les millions d’hommes, de femmes et d’enfants déplacés par ce conflit. Depuis son lancement en 2001, il est intervenu dans certaines des catastrophes les plus dévastatrices du monde, comme le tremblement de terre en Haïti (2010), la triple catastrophe au Japon (2011), les inondations en Serbie et en Bosnie-Herzégovine (2014 ), L’épidémie d’Ebola (2014), le conflit en Ukraine (2014), le tremblement de terre au Népal (2015), la crise des réfugiés en Europe et l’ouragan Matthew en Haïti (2016).
Quels que soient les événements qui surviennent, il y a une constante fiable sur laquelle vous pouvez compter: l’UE continuera à promouvoir la paix et la sécurité internationales, le multilatéralisme, l’intégration régionale, la coopération au développement, les droits de l’homme et à répondre aux crises humanitaires.
Josep Coll, Chef de délégation de l’Union européenne au Bénin

On 25 March, the European Union will mark the 60th anniversary of the signing of the Treaties of Rome, the first step towards a united Europe. Since the birth of the European Communities in 1957, Europe has known six decades of unprecedented peace, prosperity and security.

The contrast with the first half of the 20th century could not be more striking. Two catastrophic wars in Europe in 1914-18 and 1939-1945 left millions dead and a continent devastated, divided and prostrate. For countries that had long been at war, European integration has been the most successful peace project in our history.

Today, we are living in unpredictable times. The 60th anniversary of the Treaties of Rome is an opportunity not only to reaffirm our attachment to the values and objectives on which the European project is founded, but also to take pragmatic and ambitious measures.

The European Union has been present in Benin since its independence, and the partnership between the European Union and Benin has deepened over the years. Limited to cooperation in the first years and even decades, the partnership has since expanded greatly. Today we exchange regularly on questions of foreign policy, security, human rights, and also issues of global interest such as climate change and mobility.

The world is going through a period of great uncertainty. The global balance is shifting and the foundations of a rules-based international order are too often called into question. But the EU's position, for its part, provides certainties: we are defenders of better global rules, rules that protect citizens against abuse, rules that broaden rights and raise standards. It is thanks to our commitment – that of the Union and its Member States – that the world community has put in place ground-breaking agreements such as “the Sustainable Development Goals,” “the Paris Agreement on Climate Change” and “the Addis Ababa Action Agenda on Financing for Development.” In a world where power politics is emerging, the European Union will have an even more important role to play.

The European Union is and will remain a solid, cooperative and reliable partner. Our partners know our areas of activity and the values we defend. We defend multilateralism, human rights and international cooperation.

The EU is the world's second-largest economy. We are the world's largest market and the leading foreign investor in most regions of the globe. The EU has reached an influential position by acting together and with a single voice on the world stage, by playing, as a member of the World Trade Organisation, a key role in eliminating obstacles to trade, and by concluding bilateral trade agreements with many important partners – such as the recent CETA agreement with Canada. This has enabled European exporting companies to prosper and to create more than 30 million jobs.

Original copy of the Treaty of Rome

We invest more in development cooperation and humanitarian aid than the rest of the world combined. The EU is increasingly active as a global provider of security. We work for sustainable development, inclusive societies, and the fight against all inequalities – in education, democracy and human rights. The European Union is the world's leading donor of development aid. For us, this is not charity: it is a smart investment in your prosperity and stability and therefore also in our own security and prosperity.

We played a determining role in the planning of the UN's sustainable development goals and we have already implemented them, while working on updating the European Consensus on development policy. The EU's development aid goes to some 150 countries around the world and is increasingly focused on the world's poorest regions. The EU is the only donor in the world that provides its support in all fragile or conflict-affected countries.

A more fragile international environment calls for greater engagement, not retrenchment. That is why the EU will continue to support and assist the United Nations: our cooperation with the UN covers peace missions, diplomatic efforts, human rights, and the fight against hunger and crime. The European Union is also a strong and active partner of regional organisations such as the African Union, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Arctic Council.

The European Union is also ready to help people affected by natural and/or man-made disasters. Humanitarian crises continue to weigh heavily at the international level and, in 2016, the EU allocated more than 1.5 billion euros to food aid, shelter, protection and health care for 120 million people in more than 80 countries. Since the beginning of the Syrian conflict in 2011, the EU has been the largest donor of humanitarian aid for the millions of men, women and children displaced by that conflict. Since its launch in 2001, it has intervened in some of the world's most devastating disasters, such as the earthquake in Haiti (2010), the triple disaster in Japan (2011), the floods in Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina (2014), the Ebola epidemic (2014), the conflict in Ukraine (2014), the earthquake in Nepal (2015), the refugee crisis in Europe and Hurricane Matthew in Haiti (2016).

Whatever events may occur, there is one reliable constant on which you can count: the EU will continue to promote international peace and security, multilateralism, regional integration, development cooperation and human rights, and to respond to humanitarian crises.

Josep Coll, Head of the Delegation of the European Union to Benin

Dans un entretien exclusif avec Guinéenews, Sékou Yaffa Sylla, Directeur général de la Compagnie du Développement des Mines (CDM), revient sur l’engagement de son entreprise dans le secteur minier guinéen. Il présente les efforts de CDM pour devenir un acteur de renom international dans le développement des ressources de bauxite tout en respectant les normes environnementales et en soutenant les efforts de développement local des communautés riveraines. À travers cette interview, M. Sylla parle des initiatives de CDM pour minimiser l’impact environnemental, gérer les déchets, reboiser les sites miniers épuisés, et renforcer la coopération sino-guinéenne. Lire ci-dessous la vidéo intégrale de cet entretien exclusif !
Guinéenews : présentez-nous votre compagnie ?
Sékou Yaffa Sylla, Directeur général de CDM : CDM s’engage à devenir une entreprise de renommée internationale dans le développement des ressources de bauxite. La société mère, CHICO, est une entreprise publique chinoise dont le siège est situé dans la province du Henan, en Chine. CDM a été enregistrée à Conakry en mai 2008 et a obtenu en octobre 2010 la concession pour l’exploitation de la bauxite dans la région de Boké. La zone minière de CDM est située à la frontière des provinces de Boké et de Télimélé, en Guinée, avec une superficie d’environ 490 kilomètres carrés. Les réserves de bauxite dans toute la mine sont estimées à environ 1,5 milliard de tonnes. Il s’agit de bauxite du type gibbsite, avec une teneur moyenne en alumine de 40,79 %. Le projet a démarré sa production et ses opérations en mars 2017. Actuellement, CDM emploie 1 403 personnes, dont 1 273 sont des employés guinéens, représentant plus de 90 % de l’effectif. De janvier à août 2024, CDM a exporté 6,82 millions de tonnes de bauxite, et il est prévu que les exportations atteignent 10 millions de tonnes pour l’ensemble de l’année 2024.
Guinéenews : quelles sont les mesures prises pour minimiser l’impact environnemental des activités de votre entreprise ?
Sékou Yaffa Sylla : tout d’abord, CDM a créé un département de gestion HSSE (Hygiène, Sécurité, Santé et Environnement) chargé de surveiller et d’améliorer les tâches de protection de l’environnement. Ce département compte près de 100 professionnels qui surveillent en permanence la sécurité, la santé et l’environnement des mines, des routes et des communautés, réagissant rapidement aux incidents et améliorant les mesures de protection de l’environnement. Ensuite, CDM a amélioré ses procédés de production en utilisant des machines d’extraction, ce qui a permis de réduire les nuisances sonores, la poussière et les vibrations.
L’entreprise répare chaque année les routes des communautés, procède au nettoyage régulier des déchets, arrose les routes avec de nombreux camions-citernes pour réduire la poussière pendant la saison sèche, et mobilise des équipements pour désencombrer les cours d’eau pendant la saison des pluies. En outre, elle organise des sessions de sensibilisation dans les communautés sur la prévention des incendies de forêt et la protection de la biodiversité.
Guinéenews : comment vous gérez la problématique des déchets générés par vos opérations minières ?
Sékou Yaffa Sylla : tout d’abord, CDM améliore continuellement la précision des techniques géologiques en optimisant les plans d’exploitation minière, réduisant ainsi la proportion de déchets miniers à la source. Ensuite, CDM a prévu des aires de stockage dédiées aux déchets miniers, qui sont aménagées de manière professionnelle conformément aux normes de l’industrie afin d’éviter toute pollution de l’environnement.
Guinéenews : le reboisement des sites miniers après exploitation constitue l’autre casse-tête pour toutes les compagnies minières. Au niveau de CDM que faites-vous pour contribuer efficacement à la restauration ces sites déjà épuisés ?
Sékou Yaffa Sylla : CDM adhère toujours au concept de mine verte et intègre la réhabilitation des mines dans la gestion du cycle de vie complet des sites miniers. En collaborant avec des entreprises locales spécialisées dans l’environnement et avec le gouvernement, CDM a mis en place un plan complet et scientifique de restauration des mines. En partenariat avec les communautés locales, CDM a planté des cultures économiques sur certains sites miniers épuisés, contribuant ainsi à la restauration de l’environnement tout en créant des emplois pour les villageois locaux.
Guinéenews : parlez-nous de votre politique en matière de responsabilité sociale vis-à-vis des communautés locales ?
Sékou Yaffa Sylla : CDM est pleinement consciente de l’importance de remplir ses responsabilités sociales. Chaque année, elle fait don de 0,5 % de son chiffre d’affaires aux gouvernements locaux comme fonds de développement local, et fournit des fonds et une aide matérielle aux villages communautaires, tels que du riz, entre autres. En outre, chaque année, elle élabore un plan de développement communautaire, investit dans la construction d’infrastructures telles que des mosquées, des écoles, des marchés et des puits, et maintient une politique de localisation en favorisant l’emploi de personnel local, en renforçant la coopération avec les petites et moyennes entreprises locales, et plus de 90 % des employés et des achats de matériel sont réalisés selon le principe de « guinéennisation ».
Guinéenews：concrètement comment CDM collabore avec les communautés locales ?
Sékou Yaffa Sylla : en 2022, CDM a signé des accords de développement local avec le gouvernement de la ville de Kawessi, dans la province de Télimélé, et celui de la ville de Malaboya, dans la province de Boké.
CDM s’est engagé, à travers une coopération diversifiée et des actions concrètes, à renforcer les infrastructures des communautés environnantes des zones minières, à accroître l’accès des communautés aux services de base, à améliorer les capacités d’emploi, à soutenir le développement des entreprises locales, à encourager le développement agricole et la protection de l’environnement, et à aider à la gestion des catastrophes naturelles.
Guinéenews : les initiatives mises en place pour soutenir le développement économique local ; des exemples de réalisations ?
Sékou Yaffa Sylla : depuis le début de ses opérations en 2017, CDM a fait des dons cumulés de 2,5 millions de dollars américains aux gouvernements locaux pour le développement communautaire. La société a également construit un total de 53 puits d’eau potable, une école, 5 mosquées, une ferme avicole, et a réalisé environ 350 kilomètres de routes. En outre, environ 1 350 ensembles de panneaux solaires et équipements d’éclairage ont été installés, et environ 350 tonnes de riz ont été distribuées. Plus de 170 sessions de sensibilisation sur la santé, la prévention des maladies et la sécurité ont été organisées, bénéficiant à environ 10 000 personnes. De plus, l’entreprise a créé 1 300 emplois directs et 2 400 emplois indirects pour la population locale. Avec 90 % des approvisionnements réalisés localement, le transport du minerai et la sécurité routière sont confiés à des entreprises locales, contribuant ainsi de manière significative au développement socio-économique de la région.
Guinéenews：quels sont les principaux partenariats que vous avez établis avec les gouvernements ou d’autres entreprises ou sous-traitants pour faciliter vos opérations ?
Sékou Yaffa Sylla : depuis sa création, CDM a strictement respecté les exigences de l’article 107 du Code minier de la Guinée, en recherchant des entreprises guinéennes réputées, qualifiées et compétentes répondant aux exigences techniques de l’entreprise. CDM a établi de bonnes relations de collaboration avec de nombreuses entreprises guinéennes dans les domaines des services de transport, des services commerciaux, des services de sécurité routière, de l’achat de carburant ainsi que de l’achat de matériel et d’équipements. Après plusieurs années de coopération, la société a signé des contrats avec un grand nombre d’entreprises locales. Avec le développement continu de la technologie et l’amélioration des normes techniques, la demande de services de plus haut niveau fournis par les entreprises locales augmente. Cependant, certains services techniques et biens doivent encore être importés de l’étranger. À l’avenir, CDM continuera à renforcer sa coopération avec les entreprises locales et à améliorer progressivement le niveau de ses achats locaux.
Guinéenews：vos perspectives de croissance pour les prochaines années en Guinée ?
Sékou Yaffa Sylla : la Guinée dispose de ressources minérales et naturelles extrêmement riches. Avec la mise en service des projets de bauxite, de fer et d’autres ressources au cours des dernières années, je suis convaincu que l’économie guinéenne connaîtra un développement rapide dans les années à venir.
Guinéenews : les principaux objectifs à moyen et long termes que vous avez fixés pour votre société minière en Guinée ?
Sékou Yaffa Sylla : premièrement, il est essentiel de bien gérer la relation entre l’exploitation des ressources et la protection de l’environnement, en adoptant une approche écologique pour réaliser un développement durable. Deuxièmement, il faut concilier les activités de l’entreprise avec le développement des communautés, en stimulant l’emploi local et la croissance des petites et moyennes entreprises tout en poursuivant son propre développement. Troisièmement, il est important de gérer efficacement la relation entre l’environnement interne et externe de l’entreprise, en renforçant le dialogue avec le gouvernement, les syndicats et d’autres organisations, en opérant dans le respect des lois et des règlements, et en établissant une bonne gouvernance interne ainsi qu’une image externe positive.
Guinéenews : Quelles sont vos perspectives de croissance pour les prochaines années en Guinée ?
Pour le développement de cette mine, nous transitons au port Dapilon. Une superficie nous a été offerte là-bas par la SMB. Mais cette superficie ne correspond pas à l’élan futur de notre société, car la capacité de l’aire de stockage que nous avons à Dapilon est très petite. 560 mille tonnes, c’est peu. Aussi, sur les 5 postes, le chargement des bases n’a rien fonctionné. Ces dernières années nous souffrons beaucoup. Même l’accès au port, il y a de l’embouteillage. Au fond, le camion peut, des fois, garer pendant plus de deux heures. L’ensemble de toutes ces causes a poussé CDM à faire son propre port. Entre le port de Dapilon et le port de Guémé Saint-Jean.
Guinéenews：votre impression sur la coopération sino-guinéenne ?
Sékou Yaffa Sylla : la Guinée a été le premier pays d’Afrique subsaharienne à établir des relations diplomatiques avec la Chine. En 2017, la Chine et la Guinée ont signé un accord-cadre de coopération stratégique « ressources contre prêts », et en 2018, la Guinée a officiellement rejoint l’initiative « La Ceinture et la Route ». CDM a été l’une des premières entreprises chinoises à investir dans des projets de bauxite en Guinée. Avec l’approfondissement de la coopération entre les deux pays, des projets tels que Chalco, China Power Investment et Simandou ont été successivement lancés, apportant une nouvelle dynamique au développement économique de la Guinée. Je suis convaincu qu’avec le renforcement du partenariat entre nos deux pays, de nouveaux domaines de coopération seront établis dans les années à venir, ce qui favorisera le développement socio-économique de la Guinée, rendant le pays plus fort et plus indépendant en Afrique.

In an exclusive interview with Guinéenews, Sékou Yaffa Sylla, Director General of the Compagnie du Développement des Mines (CDM), discusses his company's engagement in the Guinean mining sector. He presents CDM's efforts to become an internationally renowned player in the development of bauxite resources while respecting environmental standards and supporting the local development efforts of neighbouring communities. In this interview, Mr Sylla speaks about CDM's initiatives to minimise environmental impact, manage waste, reforest depleted mining sites, and strengthen Sino-Guinean cooperation. Read below and watch the full video of this exclusive interview!

Guinéenews: Introduce your company to us.

Sékou Yaffa Sylla, Director General of CDM: CDM is committed to becoming an internationally renowned company in the development of bauxite resources. The parent company, CHICO, is a Chinese state-owned enterprise headquartered in Henan province, China. CDM was registered in Conakry in May 2008 and obtained in October 2010 the concession for bauxite mining in the Boké region. CDM's mining area is located on the border of the provinces of Boké and Télimélé, in Guinea, with a surface area of about 490 square kilometres. Bauxite reserves across the whole mine are estimated at about 1.5 billion tonnes. It is gibbsite-type bauxite, with an average alumina content of 40.79%. The project began production and operations in March 2017. Currently, CDM employs 1,403 people, of whom 1,273 are Guinean employees, representing more than 90% of the workforce. From January to August 2024, CDM exported 6.82 million tonnes of bauxite, and exports are expected to reach 10 million tonnes for the whole of 2024.

Guinéenews: What measures have been taken to minimise the environmental impact of your company's activities?

Sékou Yaffa Sylla: First of all, CDM created an HSSE (Hygiene, Safety, Health and Environment) management department responsible for monitoring and improving environmental protection tasks. This department has nearly 100 professionals who continuously monitor the safety, health and environment of the mines, roads and communities, reacting quickly to incidents and improving environmental protection measures. Next, CDM has improved its production processes by using extraction machinery, which has reduced noise, dust and vibration.

The company repairs community roads every year, carries out regular waste clean-up, waters the roads with numerous tanker trucks to reduce dust during the dry season, and mobilises equipment to clear waterways during the rainy season. In addition, it organises awareness sessions in the communities on preventing forest fires and protecting biodiversity.

Guinéenews: How do you manage the problem of waste generated by your mining operations?

Sékou Yaffa Sylla: First of all, CDM continuously improves the precision of geological techniques by optimising mining plans, thereby reducing the proportion of mining waste at the source. Next, CDM has provided dedicated storage areas for mining waste, which are laid out professionally in accordance with industry standards in order to avoid any environmental pollution.

Guinéenews: Reforestation of mining sites after extraction is the other headache for all mining companies. At CDM, what are you doing to contribute effectively to restoring these already depleted sites?

Sékou Yaffa Sylla: CDM always adheres to the concept of the green mine and integrates mine rehabilitation into the management of the full life cycle of mining sites. In collaboration with local companies specialising in the environment and with the government, CDM has put in place a comprehensive and scientific mine restoration plan. In partnership with local communities, CDM has planted cash crops on some depleted mining sites, thereby contributing to the restoration of the environment while creating jobs for local villagers.

Guinéenews: Tell us about your social responsibility policy towards local communities.

Sékou Yaffa Sylla: CDM is fully aware of the importance of fulfilling its social responsibilities. Every year it donates 0.5% of its turnover to local governments as a local development fund, and provides funds and material aid to community villages, such as rice, among other things. In addition, each year it draws up a community development plan, invests in the construction of infrastructure such as mosques, schools, markets and wells, and maintains a localisation policy by favouring the employment of local staff and strengthening cooperation with local small and medium-sized enterprises; more than 90% of employees and of equipment purchases are carried out according to the principle of "Guineanisation".

Guinéenews: Concretely, how does CDM work with local communities?

Sékou Yaffa Sylla: In 2022, CDM signed local development agreements with the government of the town of Kawessi, in Télimélé province, and that of the town of Malaboya, in Boké province.

CDM has committed, through diversified cooperation and concrete actions, to strengthening the infrastructure of the communities surrounding the mining areas, increasing communities' access to basic services, improving employment capacity, supporting the development of local businesses, encouraging agricultural development and environmental protection, and helping with the management of natural disasters.

Guinéenews: The initiatives put in place to support local economic development; examples of achievements?

Sékou Yaffa Sylla: Since operations began in 2017, CDM has made cumulative donations of 2.5 million US dollars to local governments for community development. The company has also built a total of 53 drinking-water wells, one school, 5 mosques, a poultry farm, and has built about 350 kilometres of roads. In addition, about 1,350 sets of solar panels and lighting equipment have been installed, and about 350 tonnes of rice have been distributed. More than 170 awareness sessions on health, disease prevention and safety have been organised, benefiting about 10,000 people. Moreover, the company has created 1,300 direct jobs and 2,400 indirect jobs for the local population. With 90% of supplies sourced locally, ore transport and road safety are entrusted to local companies, thereby contributing significantly to the socio-economic development of the region.

Guinéenews: What are the main partnerships you have established with governments or other companies or subcontractors to facilitate your operations?

Sékou Yaffa Sylla: Since its creation, CDM has strictly complied with the requirements of article 107 of Guinea's Mining Code, by seeking reputable, qualified and competent Guinean companies meeting the company's technical requirements. CDM has established good working relationships with many Guinean companies in the fields of transport services, commercial services, road safety services, fuel purchasing as well as the purchase of materials and equipment. After several years of cooperation, the company has signed contracts with a large number of local companies. With the continuous development of technology and the improvement of technical standards, demand for higher-level services provided by local companies is increasing. However, certain technical services and goods still have to be imported from abroad. In the future, CDM will continue to strengthen its cooperation with local companies and gradually improve the level of its local procurement.

Guinéenews: Your growth prospects for the coming years in Guinea?

Sékou Yaffa Sylla: Guinea has extremely rich mineral and natural resources. With the commissioning of bauxite, iron and other resource projects in recent years, I am convinced that the Guinean economy will experience rapid development in the years to come.

Guinéenews: The main medium- and long-term objectives you have set for your mining company in Guinea?

Sékou Yaffa Sylla: First, it is essential to properly manage the relationship between resource exploitation and environmental protection, by adopting an ecological approach to achieve sustainable development. Second, company activities must be reconciled with community development, by stimulating local employment and the growth of small and medium-sized enterprises while pursuing its own development. Third, it is important to manage effectively the relationship between the company's internal and external environment, by strengthening dialogue with the government, the unions and other organisations, operating in compliance with laws and regulations, and establishing good internal governance as well as a positive external image.

Guinéenews: What are your growth prospects for the coming years in Guinea?

For the development of this mine, we transit through the port of Dapilon. An area was granted to us there by SMB. But this area does not match our company's future momentum, because the capacity of the storage area we have at Dapilon is very small. 560 thousand tonnes is little. Also, out of the 5 berths, the loading of the bases has not worked at all. In recent years we have been suffering a great deal. Even access to the port is congested. At the bottom, a truck can sometimes be parked for more than two hours. All of these causes together pushed CDM to build its own port, between the port of Dapilon and the port of Guémé Saint-Jean.

Guinéenews: Your impression of Sino-Guinean cooperation?

Sékou Yaffa Sylla: Guinea was the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to establish diplomatic relations with China. In 2017, China and Guinea signed a "resources for loans" strategic cooperation framework agreement, and in 2018 Guinea officially joined the "Belt and Road" initiative. CDM was one of the first Chinese companies to invest in bauxite projects in Guinea. With the deepening of cooperation between the two countries, projects such as Chalco, China Power Investment and Simandou have been launched one after another, bringing new momentum to Guinea's economic development. I am convinced that with the strengthening of the partnership between our two countries, new areas of cooperation will be established in the years to come, which will promote Guinea's socio-economic development, making the country stronger and more independent in Africa.

ABU DABI (UNA/WAM) – UAE će predsjedavati Međunarodnim komitetom za vještačku inteligenciju u sistemima potrage i spašavanja. Ovo slijedi nakon objave Međunarodne organizacije Cospas-Sarsat tokom njenog virtuelnog sastanka održanog 13. juna o formiranju međunarodne radne grupe specijalizirane za primjenu vještačke inteligencije u satelitskim sistemima potrage i spašavanja. Ovo slijedi nakon velikog uspjeha sastanaka organizacije održanih u Abu Dabiju od 27. maja do 5. juna 2025. godine.
Ova odluka donesena je na osnovu radnog dokumenta koji je predstavila Komanda Nacionalne garde, koju predstavlja Nacionalni centar za traganje i spašavanje, tokom sastanaka Međunarodnog odbora, kojima su prisustvovali predstavnici 45 zemalja, zajedno s brojnim međunarodnim organizacijama, među kojima su najznačajnije Međunarodna unija za telekomunikacije (ITU), Međunarodna organizacija civilnog vazduhoplovstva (ICAO) i Međunarodna pomorska organizacija (IMO).
UAE je predložio pionirski tehnički prijedlog usmjeren na integraciju tehnologija vještačke inteligencije u operacije Centra za kontrolu misije (MCC), povećanje efikasnosti sistema za spašavanje u svemiru i poboljšanje brzine i tačnosti odgovora na pozive u pomoć putem inteligentne obrade podataka i integracije preko satelitskih mreža.
Inicijativa UAE dobila je široke pohvale država članica zbog svoje inovativnosti i naprednog pristupa, što odražava spremnost i liderstvo zemlje u podršci međunarodnim naporima za modernizaciju tehničke infrastrukture COSPAS-SARSAT sistema.
U svjetlu toga, usvojena je preporuka za formiranje zajedničke radne grupe, kojom predsjedavaju UAE, za koordinaciju tehničke saradnje između država članica i relevantnih tijela te razvoj alata vještačke inteligencije povezanih s centrima za kontrolu misije, čime se poboljšava spremnost i odziv sistema potrage i spašavanja na globalnom nivou.
Odbor je pohvalio ulogu UAE, njihov kvalitativni doprinos i proaktivne inicijative u korištenju modernih tehnologija u svrhu međunarodnih humanitarnih ciljeva spašavanja.
Ova odluka odražava napredni međunarodni ugled UAE i učvršćuje njihovu ulogu kao efikasnog strateškog partnera u budućnosti COSPAS-SARSAT sistema i razvoju njegove tehničke infrastrukture.
Novi odbor treba da uspostavi globalne standarde i pravila za integraciju vještačke inteligencije u sisteme za potragu i spašavanje u svemiru, poboljša tehničku saradnju i razmjenu stručnosti i znanja među državama članicama, te otvori članstvo subjektima koji žele da se pridruže ovoj pionirskoj međunarodnoj tehničkoj inicijativi.

ABU DHABI (UNA/WAM) – The UAE will chair the International Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Search and Rescue Systems. This follows the announcement by the Cospas-Sarsat International Organisation, during its virtual meeting held on 13 June, of the formation of a specialised international working group on the application of artificial intelligence in satellite search and rescue systems. This comes after the great success of the organisation's meetings held in Abu Dhabi from 27 May to 5 June 2025.
This decision was taken on the basis of a working paper presented by the National Guard Command, represented by the National Search and Rescue Centre, during the meetings of the International Committee, which were attended by representatives of 45 countries, along with numerous international organisations, the most prominent among them being the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the International Maritime Organization (IMO).
The UAE proposed a pioneering technical proposal aimed at integrating artificial intelligence technologies into the operations of the Mission Control Centre (MCC), increasing the efficiency of space-based rescue systems and improving the speed and accuracy of responses to distress calls through intelligent data processing and integration across satellite networks.
The UAE's initiative received wide praise from member states for its innovativeness and advanced approach, reflecting the country's readiness and leadership in supporting international efforts to modernise the technical infrastructure of the COSPAS-SARSAT system.
In light of this, a recommendation was adopted to form a joint working group, chaired by the UAE, to coordinate technical cooperation between member states and the relevant bodies and to develop artificial intelligence tools connected to mission control centres, thereby improving the readiness and responsiveness of search and rescue systems at the global level.
The Committee praised the role of the UAE, its qualitative contribution and its proactive initiatives in using modern technologies for the purposes of international humanitarian rescue objectives.
This decision reflects the UAE's advanced international standing and consolidates its role as an effective strategic partner in the future of the COSPAS-SARSAT system and the development of its technical infrastructure.
The new committee is to establish global standards and rules for the integration of artificial intelligence into space-based search and rescue systems, improve technical cooperation and the exchange of expertise and knowledge among member states, and open membership to entities wishing to join this pioneering international technical initiative.
(ends)
